tagline: Silk Road cities of blue tile
overview:
Uzbekistan lies in the heart of Central Asia, bordered by Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Afghanistan and Turkmenistan. It is one of only two countries in the world that is double landlocked, meaning every neighbor is landlocked too. Its 447,000 km², about the size of California, run from desert to the foothills of high mountains.

About 36 million people live in Uzbekistan, the most populous country in Central Asia. Uzbek is the state language and Russian is widely spoken. Tashkent, the capital, is the region's largest city, rebuilt after a 1966 earthquake and known for a subway whose stations are decorated like palaces.

Uzbekistan is a presidential republic. Cotton, gold, gas and fruit are its main products. Its greatest fame comes from the Silk Road cities of Samarkand, Bukhara and Khiva, where turquoise-tiled domes, minarets and madrasas have stood for centuries.
landAndNature: Most of Uzbekistan is flat and dry: the Kyzylkum, or red sand desert, fills the center, and steppe covers much of the rest. Mountains rise in the east toward Tajikistan and Kyrgyzstan, feeding the Amu Darya and Syr Darya rivers, whose water was diverted on a huge scale in the Soviet era to irrigate cotton. As a result the Aral Sea, once the fourth-largest lake in the world, has shrunk to a fraction of its size, leaving rusting fishing boats stranded on salty sand and a dust problem that harms local health. The Fergana Valley in the east is fertile and densely farmed, famous for melons, apricots and mulberries. Wildlife includes saiga antelope, goitered gazelles and, in the mountains, snow leopards.
peopleAndCulture: Uzbek hospitality centers on plov, rice cooked with lamb, carrots, onions and sometimes quince in a huge cast-iron kazan, prepared by men for guests and weddings. Round non bread is stamped with patterns and never set down upside down. Suzani embroidery, worked in bright silk on cotton, is made for brides, and ikat silk is dyed before weaving so its patterns blur like flames. Navruz in March brings the spring new year with music and communal cooking. Most Uzbeks are Muslim. Kurash, a traditional jacketed wrestling style, is a national sport alongside soccer, and Uzbek boxers and judoka win Olympic medals. Tea is poured, returned to the pot and poured again three times before serving, a gesture of care.
history: Cities here were stops on the Silk Road for 2,000 years, where caravans traded Chinese silk for glass, horses and ideas. Alexander the Great conquered Sogdiana in the 320s BC; Arab armies brought Islam in the 700s, and Bukhara and Samarkand became centers of science and poetry, home to the mathematician al-Khwarizmi, whose name gave us the word algorithm, and the physician Ibn Sina. Genghis Khan's Mongols destroyed the cities in the 1220s. Timur, known in Europe as Tamerlane, rebuilt Samarkand as his capital in the late 1300s, and his grandson Ulugh Beg built an observatory that measured the year to within a minute. Russia conquered the region in the 1800s, and Soviet rule from the 1920s expanded cotton farming with the irrigation that drained the Aral Sea. Uzbekistan became independent in 1991.
funFacts: Uzbekistan is one of only two double-landlocked countries on Earth; the other is Liechtenstein.
The Registan in Samarkand is a square framed by three tiled schools, once a center of astronomy and mathematics.
The Aral Sea has shrunk so far that ships now sit rusting in desert sand kilometers from any water.
The word algorithm comes from al-Khwarizmi, a mathematician from the region who worked in the 800s.
Ulugh Beg's 1400s observatory in Samarkand measured the length of a year accurate to within about a minute.
